title: Lesson 38: Case study: an org that scaled AI well
description: Grounded in Lesson 38 of the AI Adoption series: the four moves that took a mid-market logistics program from nine stalled pilots to scale, why killing failing pilots on a written gate did not cost political capital, how change capacity becomes a numeric budget, the real published bank case behind the pattern, and the difference between individual productivity and enterprise financial impact in the survey evidence.

questions.question: A use case is ready to move from a pilot to organization-wide use. Which set of conditions belongs in the scale gate?
options: Executive support, a vendor roadmap commitment, a launch date, and a completed training session
Quality on your own tasks, a named owner, a support path, and a defensible unit cost
A pilot group of at least fifty users, two quarters of data, and an approved invoice
A written policy, a communications plan, a committee vote, and a budget line
questions.explanation: A scale gate is what turns a pilot into a decision: quality measured on your own tasks, a named business owner, a support path that exists on a bad day, and a unit cost you can defend against the manual alternative. Without those four lines a use case goes wide on enthusiasm.

questions.question: What separates workflow redesign from inserting a tool into work that stays the same?
options: The tool is replaced with a more capable model at each step of the process
The team receives more training before the tool reaches the rest of the group
The process around the tool changes, so different work happens rather than faster work
The tool is given to a larger population while the underlying process is left unchanged
questions.explanation: Redesign changes the process around the tool so the work itself is different, which is where enterprise value comes from. Insertion keeps the same process and mainly makes individual tasks faster.

questions.question: A team lead says her group can absorb two process changes this quarter without service slipping. How should that number be used?
options: As a budget for new work, with anything beyond it queued and given a date
As a minimum to build on, since teams usually underestimate what they can take
As a figure to average across teams, so every group gets an equal share of work
As context for the steering group, without letting it limit the planned roadmap
questions.explanation: Change capacity is the number of process changes a team can absorb before the work it already does gets worse, and writing it down converts it into a budget. The next idea then waits in a queue with a date instead of arriving as one more request.
